derivations.claim:
For fixed $n$, the symmetric tensors are the range of the averaging
projection on $(\mathbb C^r)^{\otimes n}$. The elementary tensors in the basis
$e_1,\ldots,e_r$ span the tensor power, so their averages span that range.
Two such averages with different occupation vectors are orthogonal, because
at least one tensor slot has orthogonal basis vectors in every paired term.
For occupation vector $N$ the squared norm of the averaged tensor is
$\prod_jn_j!/n!$ by counting the $\prod_jn_j!$ permutations that preserve the
ordered occupation word among $n!$ permutations. Multiplying by
$\sqrt{n!/\prod_jn_j!}$ normalizes it. The CCR in [F2], applied successively
to the vacuum, show that this normalized vector is exactly $|N\rangle$;
therefore the vectors $|N\rangle$ are an orthonormal basis of each sector.
The sector direct sum in [F1] makes their union a complete orthonormal family
of Fock space.

The target family $(g_N)$ is complete orthonormal by [F3]. Hence the
linear map $|N\rangle\mapsto g_N$ preserves norms on finite linear
combinations, extends by completion to an isometry on Fock space, and is
surjective because its range contains the complete family $(g_N)$ and is
closed. Uniqueness follows from density of the finite span.

On a basis vector $|N\rangle$, the ladder formulas [F2] and Hermite
recurrences [F3] give
$$\mathcal U a_j\mathcal U^{-1}g_N=\sqrt{n_j}g_{N-e_j}
=\frac{x_j+\partial_{x_j}}{\sqrt2}g_N,$$
and
$$\mathcal U a_j^*\mathcal U^{-1}g_N=\sqrt{n_j+1}g_{N+e_j}
=\frac{x_j-\partial_{x_j}}{\sqrt2}g_N.$$
Linearity proves these identities on the finite span. Adding and subtracting
the two identities gives the displayed $Q_j,P_j$ formulas there. The formulas
are only asserted on this core, where all terms are defined.

On $L^2(\mathbb R^r)$, multiplication by real $x_j$ is symmetric. If $g$
lies in its adjoint domain with adjoint value $h$, testing against compactly
supported functions on each box where $x_j$ is bounded gives $h=x_jg$ almost
everywhere there; the boxes exhaust $\mathbb R^r$, so $x_jg\in L^2$ and the
adjoint domain is exactly $D(M_{x_j})$. Thus $M_{x_j}$ is self-adjoint. The
full Fourier transform is unitary by [F2]; conjugating $M_{k_j}$ by it
defines the self-adjoint operator $-i\partial_{x_j}$, since on Schwartz
functions integration by parts gives
$\mathcal F(-i\partial_{x_j}f)=k_j\mathcal Ff$. Schwartz functions are
a core for multiplication: truncate by smooth compact cutoffs and then
mollify on the resulting bounded support; dominated convergence controls
$f$ and $x_jf$, and boundedness of $x_j$ on that support controls the
mollification error. Fourier invariance of Schwartz space gives the same
core assertion for the derivative. Conjugation by $\mathcal U$ therefore
defines the stated self-adjoint quadratures and common core.

On that core, [F1] gives $Q_j=\sqrt{\hbar/2}(a_j+a_j^*)$ and
$P_j=-i\sqrt{\hbar/2}(a_j-a_j^*)$. The creation and annihilation CCR in
[F1] imply the displayed quadrature commutators by bilinearity; all products are defined on
the finite Hermite span. Direct multiplication of the formula for $W$ gives
the phase $e^{-i\hbar(q\cdot p'-p\cdot q')/2}$, which is
$e^{-i\hbar z^TJz'/2}$ in interleaved notation. Its strong continuity and
irreducibility follow from [F3] after the parameter-preserving change
$(q_0,p_0)=(-\sqrt\hbar p,q/\sqrt\hbar)$ in the root Schrödinger formula.
The real symplectic form is unchanged by that map and the central parameter
is $\hbar\ne0$. Applying [F4] proves the representation-equivalence clause
with precisely its hypotheses.

The positive trace-class spectral expansion in [F5] has weights summing
to one. For any eigenvalue $w>0$, changing the orthonormal basis of its
eigenspace changes the sum of squared norms $\sum\|R_j\psi\|^2$ by a unitary
finite-dimensional change of basis when the eigenspace is finite-dimensional;
positive trace-class compactness makes each nonzero eigenspace finite
dimensional. The same basis invariance holds for the sesquilinear cross sum
by polarization, and the zero eigenspace contributes nothing. Cauchy–Schwarz
then gives absolute convergence of each first-moment series and of each
cross-moment series under the stated second-moment bound. Thus the definitions
of $d,V$ are finite and basis independent; taking the real part makes
$V_{jk}=V_{kj}\in\mathbb R$. Finally, every finite-dimensional cutoff of
Fock space has finite matrix dimension, and for square matrices $A,B$,
$\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$ by expanding the diagonal entries, whereas the
identity has positive trace. Hence a finite cutoff cannot satisfy the exact
CCR $[Q_j,P_j]=i\hbar I$.

$$\mathcal F W(q,p)\mathcal F^*=W(p,-q).$$

A density operator is a positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with

each eigenspace. The state is Gaussian when its Weyl characteristic function
has the form
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho W(z))= \exp\!\left(i z^Td-\tfrac12z^TVz\right)\quad(z\in\mathbb R^{2r}),$$

number truncation is used.

of the following three types and their inverses:
$$U_X=\begin{pmatrix}I&X\\0&I\end{pmatrix},\quad L_Y=\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\Y&I\end{pmatrix},\quad D_A=\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\0&A^{-T}\end{pmatrix},$$

Differentiating the determinant by its finite polynomial formula gives $(\det F)'=(\det F)\operatorname{tr}(F^{-1}\dot F)$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

define the self-adjoint quadratures

in grouped order $(q,p)$ whose upper-right block $B$ is invertible. Consider

Define $\operatorname{Mp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ as the set of endpoints of the normalized evolutions in [F4] along piecewise-smooth coefficient paths $K(t)=K(t)^T$, with $H_t=\tfrac14\sum_{j,k}K_{jk}(t)(R_jR_k+R_kR_j)$ and no linear or scalar term. The operator acts on the common Schwartz space. Concatenation gives products: first evolve by $U_2$, then evolve by $U_1$ with its initial vector $U_2f$, obtaining $U_1U_2$. The reversed evolution $U(T-t)U(T)^{-1}$ starts at $I$, ends at $U(T)^{-1}$, and is generated by $-H_{T-t}$, so inverses also belong to the set. By [F4], each endpoint implements the symplectic solution $\dot S=J_0K(t)S$. If two matrices had the same implementing unitary, differentiating their Weyl covariances on Schwartz space would give $(S-S')R=0$. Applied to the vacuum, $Q_kg_0=\sqrt{\hbar/2}g_{e_k}$ and $P_kg_0=i\sqrt{\hbar/2}g_{e_k}$ by [F6]; the reality of the rows forces both their position and momentum coefficients to vanish. Thus the endpoint is unique. For two lifts, $\pi(M_1M_2)=\pi(M_1)\pi(M_2)$ by conjugating the quadratures, so $\pi$ is a homomorphism.

Every generator from [F2] is a path endpoint of a homogeneous quadratic Hamiltonian. A symmetric shear is joined to the identity by scaling its symmetric block, and a partial Fourier rotation is joined by varying the oscillator angle. If $\det A>0$, polar decomposition writes $A=OP$ with $O\in SO(r)$ and $P$ positive definite. The path $P_t=(1-t)I+tP$ stays positive definite, and an orthogonal matrix in $SO(r)$ is a product of plane rotations, each joined to the identity by varying its angle. These paths connect the coordinate change to the identity. If $\det A<0$, factor one coordinate reflection from a positive-determinant change; that reflection is a $\pi$ oscillator rotation on that mode. This gives a piecewise-smooth symplectic path for each generator. Along any such path $S_t$, the matrix $X_t=\dot S_tS_t^{-1}$ satisfies $X_t^TJ_0+J_0X_t=0$; hence $K_t=-J_0X_t$ is symmetric and $\dot S_t=J_0K_tS_t$. The symmetrically ordered quadratic with matrix $K_t$ therefore has this classical endpoint. Thus [F2] supplies, for every $S$, a product of normalized quadratic propagators whose endpoint is $S$, proving $\pi$ is onto. The one-parameter paths also show that each such product belongs to the identity component of $\operatorname{Mp}$.

If $M_1,M_2$ implement the same $S$, then [F3] makes $M_2M_1^*=\lambda I$ for some $|\lambda|=1$. For any other representation $W'$ in [F1], choose a unitary $V$ with $VW'(z)V^*=W(z)$ by the finite-dimensional Stone–von Neumann theorem. Then $M'_S=V^*M_SV$ is unitary and $$M_S'^*W'(z)M'_S=V^*M_S^*W(z)M_SV=W'(S^Tz).$$ Conjugating the phase-uniqueness statement by $V$ proves the same result in that representation.

If two normalized lifts lie over the same grouped matrix $S$, the Gaussian determinant calculation in [F5] makes them differ by sign. This already holds for every $S$: the matrix $A+iB$ used there is invertible by symplecticity, including when either real block is singular. In particular it supplies the required invertible-$B$ chart argument without an imported Maslov-index parity formula. Thus every fiber has at most two elements.

The identity has two distinct lifts. The constant zero Hamiltonian gives $I$. On the first mode (and as the identity on the other modes if $r>1$), take the canonical Schwartz evolution of $H=\hbar(N+1/2)$ constructed in [F4]. For each Hermite vector, $e^{-it(n+1/2)}|n\rangle$ solves the same Schrödinger equation with that initial vector, so uniqueness in [F4] identifies $U(t)|n\rangle=e^{-it(n+1/2)}|n\rangle$. Then $\widetilde M_S$ and $-\widetilde M_S$ are two distinct lifts; step 2.3 proves there are no others. The kernel is exactly $\{I,-I\}$.

Fix $S_0$ and a normalized lift $M_0$. On a matrix neighborhood $\mathcal B$ of $S_0$ small enough that $SS_0^{-1}$ lies in the local neighborhood of [F4], put $\sigma(S)=L(SS_0^{-1})M_0$. The parameter path $(Y,A,X)\mapsto(\tau Y,I+\tau(A-I),\tau X)$ in [F4] joins each local factor lift to $I$ smoothly, with homogeneous quadratic logarithmic generator. Thus the local factors are endpoints of the piecewise-smooth class defining this group, so $\sigma(S)$ belongs to $\operatorname{Mp}$ and has endpoint $S$. Conversely the construction of [F4] writes any integrable-coefficient propagator endpoint as a finite product of these same local lifts. Hence allowing the broader integrable temporal class in the parity lemma introduces no additional endpoint operators or phases. It depends continuously on $S$, as does its inverse, pointwise in the Schwartz topology: the explicit chirp and linear-coordinate factors have uniformly bounded seminorm estimates on compact parameter neighborhoods, and the Fourier factors are fixed continuous maps. These estimates also justify continuity when composing such a varying local factor with a varying Schwartz vector. Step 3.1 shows every lift over $S$ is exactly $\sigma(S)$ or $-\sigma(S)$.

The endpoint map is continuous for the specified operator topology, without assuming joint continuity of arbitrary Schwartz-operator composition. For each row $j$ and mode $k$, covariance and [F6] give $\langle R_jMg_0,Mg_{e_k}\rangle=\sqrt{\hbar/2}(S_{j,Q_k}+iS_{j,P_k})$, where the pairing is linear in its first argument. On the left $R_j$ is continuous on Schwartz space, its inclusion into $L^2$ is continuous, and only the two fixed input vectors $g_0,g_{e_k}$ are used. Thus every real matrix entry of $\pi(M)$ is continuous. Over $\mathcal B$, the scalar $\varepsilon(M):=\langle Mg_0,\sigma(\pi(M))g_0\rangle$ is continuous, takes exactly the values $+1,-1$, and distinguishes the two lifts since $\|g_0\|=1$. Therefore the two inverse images $\varepsilon^{-1}(1)$ and $\varepsilon^{-1}(-1)$ in $\pi^{-1}(\mathcal B)$ are disjoint open sheets; on each, $\pi$ and $\pm\sigma$ are continuous inverse maps onto $\mathcal B$. This proves the two-fold covering in the given topology.

The same charts make the set a topological group. Locally its elements are $\varepsilon\sigma(S)$. Products and inverses of their explicit finite-parameter factors depend continuously on the matrix parameters and on each Schwartz vector, by the uniform seminorm bounds in step 4.1; their endpoint matrices multiply and invert continuously. The sign relative to a local section at the resulting endpoint is recovered by the continuous vacuum pairing in step 5.1. Hence multiplication and inversion are continuous in these charts, which have precisely the operator topology by step 5.1. Finally every defining normalized path is continuous in that topology by [F4], including its inverse path, so it joins its endpoint to $I$. Consequently the group is path connected. Together with step 3.1 this proves the connected double cover with kernel $\{I,-I\}$ and its defining unitary action, retaining the unrestricted phase ambiguity only for arbitrary individual Weyl implementers.

Then the $a'_j$ satisfy $[a'_j,(a'_k)^*]=\delta_{jk}I$ and
$[a'_j,a'_k]=0$ on that core. The real matrix
$$S_g=\begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{Re}(U+V)&-\operatorname{Im}(U-V)\\
\operatorname{Im}(U+V)&\operatorname{Re}(U-V)\end{pmatrix}$$

Then $(|N\rangle)_N$ and $(g_N)_N$ are complete orthonormal families, and the

$$\mathcal U:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^r).$$

A change of variables gives
$$\int_{\mathbb R}|U_sf(x)|^2dx
=\int_{\mathbb R}|f(y)|^2dy,$$
so $U_s$ is unitary. The chain rule for $Q=\sqrt\hbar x$ and
$P=-i\sqrt\hbar\partial_x$ gives
$U_s^*aU_s=\cosh(s)a+\sinh(s)a^*$. The scalar pair obeys
$|u|^2-|v|^2=1$ and $uv=vu$. For the $N$-mode product take
$U_N=uI_N$ and $V_N=vI_N$; the finite Bogoliubov result [F1] supplies an
implementer for these coefficients. Write
$\psi_s(x)=U_sg_0(x)=e^{-s/2}\pi^{-1/4}e^{-e^{-2s}x^2/2}$. Then
$$a\psi_s=\frac{1-e^{-2s}}{\sqrt2}x\psi_s,\qquad
\|a\psi_s\|^2=\frac{(1-e^{-2s})^2}{2}\frac{e^{2s}}2=\sinh^2(s),$$
because the probability density $|\psi_s|^2$ has second position moment
$e^{2s}/2$. By [F3], the $N$-mode Fock–Schrödinger unitary sends its vacuum
$\Omega_N$ to $g_0^{\otimes N}$. On $L^2(\mathbb R^N)$ define
$$[U_s^{(N)}f](x_1,\ldots,x_N)=e^{-Ns/2}
f(e^{-s}x_1,\ldots,e^{-s}x_N).$$
Changing variables in all $N$ coordinates proves this is unitary. It is the
product of the one-mode dilations, and the coordinatewise chain rule gives
$U_s^{(N)*}a_jU_s^{(N)}=u a_j+v a_j^*$ for each $j$. The finite Bogoliubov
statement [F1] also supplies an implementer for this coefficient pair. Put
$\Psi_N=(U_s\Omega)^{\otimes N}$ under the same identification; its $j$th
number expectation is the one-mode value $\|a\psi_s\|^2=\sinh^2(s)$ already
computed above. The number operator is the sum of the $N$ mode number
operators, so linearity gives
$$\langle\Psi_N,\mathcal N_N\Psi_N\rangle=N\sinh^2(s).$$
The product unitary exists because it is the tensor product of finitely many
copies of this unitary. The same coefficient pair is covered by the finite
Bogoliubov statement [F2]; no infinite product is taken.

In Schrödinger coordinates, $\Omega=g_0$ and
$U_sg_0(x)=e^{-s/2}\pi^{-1/4}e^{-e^{-2s}x^2/2}$. Direct Gaussian integration
gives
$$\langle g_0,U_sg_0\rangle
=\pi^{-1/2}e^{-s/2}\int_{\mathbb R}
e^{-(1+e^{-2s})x^2/2}\,dx
=\sqrt{\frac{2}{e^s+e^{-s}}}=\frac1{\sqrt{\cosh s}}.$$
Since $U_s$ and $g_0$ are real and positive here, this is also the overlap
magnitude; the formula holds for every real $s$. Product inner products
factor over the $N$ modes, yielding
$$|\langle\Omega_N,\Psi_N\rangle|=(\cosh s)^{-N/2}.$$
For $s\ne0$, $\cosh s>1$, so this magnitude tends to zero as $N\to\infty$.
Together with step 1.1 this proves only the stated finite-$N$ divergence and
overlap limit. Finite-dimensional implementation does not itself provide an
infinite-mode implementer, and this example does not prove that none exists.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, an integer $r\ge1$, and an action scale
$\hbar>0$. Inner products are linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]]). Use the Fock-to-Schrödinger unitary
$\mathcal U:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)\to L^2(\mathbb R^r)$ of
[[lem-nrqmx-finite-mode-fock-schr-identification]]. In Schrödinger coordinates
define the self-adjoint quadratures
$$Q_j=\mathcal U^{-1}(\sqrt\hbar\,x_j)\mathcal U,\qquad P_j=\mathcal U^{-1}(-i\sqrt\hbar\,\partial_{x_j})\mathcal U,$$
where $x_j$ is the real multiplication operator on its maximal domain and
$-i\partial_{x_j}$ is defined by conjugating that multiplication operator by
the unitary Fourier transform. Their common Schwartz core satisfies
$$[Q_j,Q_k]=[P_j,P_k]=0,\qquad [Q_j,P_k]=i\hbar\delta_{jk}I.$$
Write $R=(Q_1,P_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_r)^T$ and
$J=\bigoplus_{j=1}^r\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.
The Weyl unitary labelled by $z=(q_1,p_1,\ldots,q_r,p_r)$ is the unitary
whose grouped-coordinate formula, with $q=(q_1,\ldots,q_r)$ and
$p=(p_1,\ldots,p_r)$, is
$$[W(z)f](x)=e^{i\sqrt\hbar\,q\cdot(x+\sqrt\hbar p/2)}f(x+\sqrt\hbar p).$$
It obeys $W(z)W(z')=e^{-i\hbar z^TJz'/2}W(z+z')$ and is regular and
irreducible. By the finite-dimensional Stone–von Neumann theorem, every
nonzero irreducible regular Weyl system with this finite phase space and this
same nonzero central parameter is unitarily equivalent to it.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

1. $E_k[H^k]=\{u_f:f\in W^{k,2}\}$, and
   $\Phi(f):=E_k^{-1}(u_f)$ is a bijection
   $\Phi:W^{k,2}\to H^k$. Thus, under the regular-distribution embedding,
   $W^{k,2}$ and $H^k$ are the same subspace of $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.
2. There are constants $0<c_k\le C_k<\infty$, depending only on $n$ and $k$,
   with
$$c_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2\le\|f\|_{W^{k,2}} \le C_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2,$$
   and $\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2=\|\Phi(f)\|_{H^k}$. Hence the
   weak-derivative norm and the bracket-weighted $L^2$ norm are equivalent,
   and the latter is also equivalent to
   $\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}\mathcal F_2f\|_2$, by
$$\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2\le\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}h\|_2 \le(2\pi)^k\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2,\qquad h\in L^2 .$$

Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\eta\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. For
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, suppose that for every $\gamma\le\alpha$ there is
$v_\gamma\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$D^\gamma u=v_\gamma$ weakly. Then $\eta u$ has a weak $\alpha$-derivative,
and its almost-everywhere class is
$$D^\alpha(\eta u)=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\eta)D^{\alpha-\beta}u\quad\text{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
where $D^\beta\eta$ is the classical derivative and products are pointwise
products of representatives. The resulting class does not depend on the
representatives.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^r)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$,
$\chi=1$ on $\overline B_1(0)$, and support in $B_2(0)$ by [F3]. For
$R\ge1$ set $\chi_R(x)=\chi(x/R)$ and $f_R=\chi_Rf$. Then
$|\partial_j\chi_R|\le C/R$. By [F4], $f_R\in W^{1,2}$ and
$$\partial_j(f_R-f)=(\chi_R-1)\partial_jf+(\partial_j\chi_R)f.$$
The first terms in $f_R-f$, $x_j(f_R-f)$, and
$(\chi_R-1)\partial_jf$ tend to zero in $L^2$ by dominated convergence [F6],
since $\chi_R\to1$ pointwise and $|\chi_R-1|\le1$. The remaining derivative
term has norm at most $C\|f\|_2/R$. Thus $\|f_R-f\|_{\mathrm{quad}}\to0$.

Fix $R$ so the preceding error is below $\varepsilon/2$. The function
$f_R$ is supported in $\overline B_{2R}(0)$. By [F5], choose
$\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^r)$ with $\|\phi-f_R\|_{W^{1,2}}$ as small
as needed. Choose $\theta\in C_c^\infty$ equal to $1$ on
$\overline B_{2R}(0)$ and supported in $B_{2R+2}(0)$ by [F3], and put
$g=\theta\phi$. Since $\theta f_R=f_R$, the weak product rule [F4] gives
$$g-f_R=\theta(\phi-f_R),\qquad
\partial_j(g-f_R)=\theta\partial_j(\phi-f_R)+(partial_j\theta)(\phi-f_R).$$
The bounded derivatives of $\theta$ make the $W^{1,2}$ norm of $g-f_R$ at
most a fixed constant times $\|\phi-f_R\|_{W^{1,2}}$. Both $g$ and $f_R$
are supported in $\overline B_{2R+2}(0)$, so
$$\|x_j(g-f_R)\|_2\le(2R+2)\|g-f_R\|_2.$$
Choose $\phi$ close enough that $\|g-f_R\|_{\mathrm{quad}}<\varepsilon/2$.
Then $g\in C_c^\infty\subset\mathcal S$ and
$\|g-f\|_{\mathrm{quad}}<\varepsilon$ by step 1.1. Since $f$ and
$\varepsilon>0$ were arbitrary, $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ is dense in $D$.
